samples.text:
The two pie charts show the percentage of money that households in one country spent on different things in 1980 and in 2020.

In 1980, food was the biggest part of spending with 31%. Housing was 19% and other items was 17%. Transport took 13%, clothing 11% and leisure was the smallest with 9%. So food and housing was together half of the spending in that year.

In 2020, there was some big changes. Housing became the largest expense, it rose to 33%. On the other hand, the spending on food went down to 14%, which is less than half of 1980. Leisure also increased and it was 18%, so it doubled. Transport went up a little to 15%. However, clothing decreased from 11% to 5% and other items decreased slightly to 15%.

Overall, in 1980 people spend most of their money on food, but in 2020 housing was the most important. Also people spent more money for leisure and less money for clothes than before.
samples.why: Accurate figures for every category · simple overview at the end · repetitive linking and verbs (increased, decreased) · adequate vocabulary · several agreement, tense and preposition errors that do not affect understanding.

samples.text:
The pie charts compare how households in one country divided their spending between six categories in 1980 and 2020.

Overall, the proportion of household budgets spent on housing and leisure increased significantly over the forty years, while the share allocated to food and clothing fell. As a result, housing replaced food as the largest area of expenditure.

In 1980, food accounted for almost a third of household spending (31%), making it the biggest single item. Housing came second at 19%, followed by other items at 17%. Transport, clothing and leisure represented smaller shares, at 13%, 11% and 9% respectively.

By 2020, the picture had changed considerably. Spending on housing had risen to 33%, while the share devoted to food had more than halved, dropping to 14%. Leisure also saw a notable increase, doubling to 18%. In contrast, households spent a smaller proportion on clothing, which fell from 11% to 5%. The remaining categories changed only slightly, with transport rising to 15% and other items decreasing to 15%, so these two categories had exactly the same share in 2020.
samples.why: Clear overview identifying the main shifts · key features highlighted with accurate figures · logical structure · good range of cohesive devices and collocations (allocated to, share devoted to) · mostly error-free.

samples.text:
The charts illustrate the proportion of household expenditure that went on six categories of goods and services in one country in 1980 and 2020.

The most significant development was a reversal in the relative importance of food and housing: food was the largest expense in 1980, whereas housing had become dominant by 2020. Leisure also gained ground considerably, while clothing became a relatively minor item.

In 1980, food consumed 31% of household budgets, well ahead of housing, which accounted for 19%. Miscellaneous items made up 17%, and the remaining spending was split fairly evenly between transport (13%), clothing (11%) and leisure (9%).

Four decades later, housing costs absorbed a third of all spending (33%), an increase of 14 percentage points, while the share devoted to food had fallen to 14%, less than half its earlier level. Leisure spending doubled to 18%, overtaking both transport and other items, whereas clothing shrank from 11% to just 5%. Transport and other items, by contrast, remained broadly stable, at 15% each, which suggests that the major shifts were concentrated in essentials such as food and shelter, as well as in discretionary leisure spending.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected and grouped · clear, well-placed overview · precise comparative figures (14 points, doubled) · smooth cohesion · sophisticated vocabulary used naturally · wide range of accurate structures.
